lawyer: Mr. Jamiruddin Sircar, Advocate ----- For the Petitioners.
parties:
Afsar Ali Chowdhury and others ----- Petitioners
Vs.
The People's Republic of Bangladesh ----- Opposite Party
full_judgment:
3. During the pendency of the suit the defendant filed an application for rejection of the plaint stating that the plaintiff opposite party filed a criminal case before the magistrate being 410C/82 which was subsequently transferred to the Sessions Judge being Sessions Case No. 77 of 1983 which was quashed by the High Court, Rangpur Division in Criminal Revision No. 42 of 1984. The defendant opposite parties have since delivered the rice to Mr. Abdus Samad, the then Food officer of Akhanagar but those were not shown delivery by the said officer. Consequently, the defendant No. 2 filed a Criminal Case against the said Md. Abdus Samad before the Magistrate, Court, Thakurgaon being case No. 673 of 1983 under sections 409/420 of the Penal Code. The suit therefore with taking into consideration the delivery of the rice by the defendant, is not maintainable. It is further stated that the plaintiff has stated in paragraph No. 3 of the plaint that the cause of action arose on 30.6.83 but the suit was filed on 17.4,90 and as such the suit is hopelessly barred by limitation. 

 5. Mr. Jamiruddin Sircar, the learned Counsel who moved this application submitted that the application under Order 7 rule 11 was rejected by the Court on a misconception of law and therefore, the said need be set aside. In elaborating this point the learned Advocate submitted that the suit being money suit arising out of a contract, Article 149 of the Limitation Act is not applicable and as such the learned Subordinate Judge has committed an error of law in not considering the suit to be barred and the impugned order is therefore liable to be set aside. He has further submitted that Article 27 of the Constitution has provided that all citizens are equal before the law and entitled to equal protection of law, so no specific privilege can be offered to the Government in Civil litigation and thus 3 Years limitation in matters like this would be applicable, irrespective of position of the parties. It is further case of the learned Advocate that the court erred in law in not considering that the Limitation Act specifically provided limitation of three years in matters like this and the court erred in not considering that Article 148 and 149 of the Limitation Act is not applicable in the instant case. It is the further case that Article 149 is discriminatory. 

 7. In that case under report the facts were that as Famine conditions were prevailing, the Society was supplying food stuff at control rate. The Government advanced a sum of Rs. 3000.00 for the purpose of increasing the stock position of the Society. The Society undertook to refund the said amount on demand but they failed to repay after repeated demands and the Government filed the suit after 6 years of the date of advance. The Court found that it is clear that the Government had not engaged itself in advancing money in any commercial undertaking, trade or business but it was doing an act incidental to its function and finding so the Court held that it being a suit by the State and not by an individual while engaged in a commercial undertaking, Article 149 of the Limitation Act, which provides that all suits by Government or on behalf of the Government be filed within sixty years, would be applicable and hence found the suit not barred by limitation. 

 8. We have examined the submission of the learned Advocate and also examined the impugned judgment and it is seen that the instant Money Suit has been instituted by the plaintiff being the People's Republic of Bangladesh represented by the District Controller of Food for realisation of specific amount of money as the alleged misappropriated price of short delivery and that suit, it was found by the court below, having been filed by the Government and on behalf of the Government, the limitation would be 60 years as under Article 149 of the Limitation Act. 

 9. It is the contention of the learned Counsel that Article 149 of the Limitation Act allowing 60 Years limitation is discriminatory and it is violative of the equal protection clause of Article 27 of Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh. 

 10. We find no substance in that contention. Under the Constitution all citizens are equal before the law and have the right of equal protection under the law. The State is a person and Juristic person and as a modern welfare State it has more economic functions now a days than political. It no longer exists only to declare war or conclude treaties but it rather manages the everyday life of its citizens, education, food, shelter and the like and in exercising those economic functions of the State the State is not engaging itself in any commercial undertaking, trade or business like a citizen but would be discharging functions which are incidental to its function as a State and thus a sovereign function. These sovereign functions of the State even when dealing with commerce, trade and matters of that nature, is different from the facts of an individual dealing in such matters. Hence, the equality clause between citizens cannot be relied upon in challenging Article 149 of the Limitation Act, allowing State to file any suits within 60 years after the cause of action has arisen, to be discriminatory being violative of the equality clause. 

 11. Article 149 of the Limitation Act of course had provided for the State a long lease of life in filing suits but this the legislature did consciously considering the States limitations as a litigant, who exercises its executive function through officers subordinate to it, classifying it from others, rather, as a slow moving juristic person. This classification of the State appears to be rational, reasonable and not arbitratory. 

 13. There is also no warrant for the view that the moment the State does an act in trade or engages itself in trade or commerce or gives agricultural loan or distributes rice, and food stuff through ration dealers or manages public transport service, it ceased to function as a State and roses the classified protection as under Article 149 of the Limitation Act. None of the functions of the State and its Government are non-sovereign functions, be it economic or political, contractual or statutory except in a case where the persons doing the State function steps beyond the authority and a frolic on its own.
